title: Journeys of Paul
scope: Three conventional missionary journey groupings in Acts 13-21 and a separately labelled prisoner voyage to Rome in Acts 27-28.
method: Acts is primary for the narrated movements. Each entry is an editorial paraphrase with a passage link; no Bible text is bundled. Markers are rounded Pleiades representative points. Regions, unnamed settings and offshore passages have no invented pins. Dashed connectors join only consecutive mapped entries within one journey and are not roads or sailing tracks. First- and second-journey stages also carry original Scripture study contexts; related texts support reading without establishing precise travel dates or routes.
review: AI-assisted editorial source and reference screening. All 83 Pauline stages now have original passage-focused study context and canonical cross-references. The third journey and prisoner voyage explicitly distinguish named landfalls, inferred routes and intended destinations. Independent historical and textual specialist review has not occurred.
chronology: The timeline counts narrative stages, not elapsed time. No absolute years are assigned. Acts and Pauline-letter chronology require separate comparison; letters are not silently used to add unnamed Acts stops.

journeys.title: First missionary journey
journeys.scope: Antioch, Cyprus and southern Anatolia, returning to the sending church.
journeys.note: Acts does not number missionary journeys. This familiar grouping is an editorial study convention, following the narrated departure and return.

journeys.title: Second missionary journey
journeys.scope: Anatolia, Macedonia and Achaia, then a return towards Antioch.
journeys.note: The church visit in Acts 18:22 remains unnamed. No conjectural Jerusalem stop is mapped.

journeys.title: Third missionary journey
journeys.scope: Regional revisits, Ephesus, Macedonia and Greece, followed by the voyage to Jerusalem.
journeys.note: Regional summaries do not identify every city. This grouping ends with arrival in Jerusalem. The later prisoner voyage is presented separately as Voyage to Rome; the intervening arrest and imprisonment are not mapped here.

journeys.title: Voyage to Rome
journeys.scope: A prisoner transfer, storm, Malta wintering and arrival in Rome in Acts 27-28.
journeys.note: This is not labelled a fourth missionary journey. The embarkation at Caesarea follows the preceding custody narrative; Acts 27:1-2 itself does not name the departure port. Phoenix is an intended winter harbour, not a reached stop. Adramyttium and Alexandria describe ships, not visits by Paul.

places.name: Antioch in Syria

events.title: Sent from Antioch
events.summary: Barnabas and Saul are commissioned after worship, fasting and prayer.

study.context: Acts opens the mission in an existing community of prophets and teachers, rather than with Paul travelling alone. Worship and the church's sending establish the shared responsibility behind the later report.

events.title: Departure from Seleucia
events.summary: The travellers leave the Syrian coast for Cyprus.

study.context: Seleucia is the departure point after Antioch's commissioning. The verse is a travel transition; proclamation that follows in Cyprus supplies the next narrated activity, not an unreported teaching episode at the port.

events.title: Proclamation at Salamis
events.summary: They teach in the synagogues, assisted by John.

study.context: At Salamis the travellers proclaim the word in Jewish synagogues, with John assisting. The scene establishes their initial audience and team before the confrontation at Paphos elsewhere on Cyprus.

events.title: Across the island
events.summary: The narrative summarises travel across Cyprus towards Paphos.

study.context: Luke compresses the passage across Cyprus into a statement that they traversed the island. Paphos is named as the destination, but the intervening settlements and roads are not listed.

events.title: Before the proconsul
events.summary: Paul confronts Elymas; Sergius Paulus responds to the teaching.

study.context: Sergius Paulus seeks to hear the message, while Elymas opposes the missionaries. The episode links proclamation, resistance and the proconsul's response, rather than supplying a separate journey outside Cyprus.

events.title: Arrival at Perga
events.summary: John leaves the company and returns to Jerusalem.
events.qualification: John's return is not plotted as a journey made by Paul.

study.context: At Perga, John Mark departs for Jerusalem. The later dispute over taking him on another journey gives this separation narrative significance, without proving additional stops in Pamphylia.

events.title: Teaching in Pisidian Antioch
events.summary: Paul addresses the synagogue; the subsequent response brings both interest and opposition.

study.context: Paul's synagogue speech recalls Israel's history, David and the announced forgiveness through Jesus. The next Sabbath brings a mixed response and opposition, shaping the turn to Gentile hearers.

events.title: An extended stay at Iconium
events.summary: Teaching, a divided response and threatened violence precede departure.

study.context: At Iconium both Jews and Greeks believe, while opposition divides the city. The missionaries remain for a time before threats cause them to leave; Acts does not provide the exact duration.

events.title: Healing and conflict at Lystra
events.summary: A healing is followed by mistaken divine honours and violence against Paul.

study.context: After a man is healed at Lystra, the crowd mistakes the missionaries for gods. Their response points to the living Creator, and the ensuing attack reverses the crowd's apparent enthusiasm.

events.title: Making disciples at Derbe
events.summary: Paul and Barnabas teach and make disciples before beginning their return.

study.context: Derbe is the final named ministry town before the mission retraces its steps. Acts reports many disciples being made here, but gives no particular meeting place or length of residence.

events.title: Return to Lystra
events.summary: The return visits strengthen disciples and establish local leadership.
events.qualification: These named revisits are retained separately from the outward visits.

study.context: Returning to Lystra after persecution allows the travellers to strengthen new believers instead of leaving them isolated. Acts associates this work with encouragement amid suffering and appointing elders.

events.title: Return to Iconium
events.summary: The return visits strengthen disciples and establish local leadership.
events.qualification: These named revisits are retained separately from the outward visits.

study.context: The second visit to Iconium belongs to the pastoral return, rather than a second outward mission. Acts explicitly describes revisiting disciples and organising churches established earlier.

events.title: Return to Pisidian Antioch
events.summary: The return visits strengthen disciples and establish local leadership.
events.qualification: These named revisits are retained separately from the outward visits.

study.context: The return to Pisidian Antioch follows the opposition narrated in Acts 13. Re-entering a community despite hostility illustrates the continuing care given to new disciples beyond initial proclamation.

events.title: Return through Pisidia
events.summary: The narrative describes the regional passage on the return.

study.context: Acts says the travellers passed through Pisidia towards Pamphylia. This is a regional transition rather than an independently recorded stop in a newly named city or proof of the exact road.

events.title: Return into Pamphylia
events.summary: The regional sequence leads back towards Perga.

study.context: Pamphylia is named as a region on the return journey. The next explicit preaching action occurs at Perga; a chain of additional towns cannot be inferred solely from the regional label.

events.title: Teaching again at Perga
events.summary: The travellers proclaim the message before going down to Attalia.

study.context: Perga appears again, now with an explicit statement that the word was spoken there. The contrast with the brief outward arrival explains why the visits are retained as separate study stages.

events.title: Sailing from Attalia
events.summary: The port precedes the return sailing to Antioch.

study.context: After Perga the missionaries descend to Attalia and set sail towards Syria. The text identifies the port and destination, but not the exact sea course or stops between them.

events.title: Report to the sending church
events.summary: Paul and Barnabas recount their work and remain with the disciples.

study.context: The sending church hears what happened through the missionaries and how a door of faith opened to Gentiles. This report completes the narrative mission unit and returns the focus to the Antioch community.

events.title: A new departure
events.summary: Paul chooses Silas after the disagreement with Barnabas.
events.qualification: Barnabas and Mark sail to Cyprus separately; that journey is not assigned to Paul.

study.context: Paul proposes revisiting earlier communities, but disagreement over John Mark divides the teams. Silas accompanies Paul; the separate Barnabas-and-Mark voyage must not be treated as another Pauline stop.

events.title: Strengthening regional churches
events.summary: Paul travels through Syria and Cilicia.

study.context: Acts describes strengthening churches through Syria and Cilicia without enumerating each town or road. The regional label establishes purpose, not a licence to invent settlement-level map markers.

events.title: Derbe revisited
events.summary: The next named city in the narrated journey is Derbe.

study.context: Returning to Derbe joins the second journey to believers established on the earlier visit. Acts 16:1 names Derbe and Lystra before introducing Timothy, but not a surveyed road between them.

events.title: Timothy joins the mission
events.summary: The Lystra setting introduces Timothy and his participation.

study.context: Timothy is already a respected disciple when he joins the team. The journey also communicates the Jerusalem decisions to churches, presenting a cooperative mission rather than one person's travel log.

events.title: Through Phrygia and Galatia
events.summary: Regional travel continues while preaching in Asia is restricted.
events.qualification: The restriction is not a denial of the later recorded visit to Ephesus.

study.context: The travellers pass through Phrygia and Galatia while being restrained from speaking in Asia at that point. Luke does not name a chain of towns in this region; later Ephesus activity does not erase this earlier restriction.

events.title: A redirected journey
events.summary: An attempted move towards Bithynia is prevented; the route turns towards Troas.

study.context: An attempted entry into Bithynia is prevented and the party proceeds towards Troas. The narrative is about redirection, not an accomplished visit to Bithynia or a fully specified road through Mysia.

events.title: The Macedonian vision
events.summary: Paul receives a vision and the company prepares to cross into Macedonia.

study.context: At Troas the night vision leads the travellers to seek passage into Macedonia. The shift to 'we' narration in Acts is a literary feature, not independent evidence identifying every companion.

events.title: Via Samothrace
events.summary: The sailing narrative names Samothrace before Neapolis.

study.context: Samothrace appears in a short sea-crossing itinerary. Acts does not describe an independent preaching episode there, and an island-scale map point does not establish a specific harbour or landing.

events.title: Arrival at Neapolis
events.summary: The company reaches the Macedonian coastal town.

study.context: Neapolis is the named arrival point before travelling inland to Philippi. The passage supplies an ordered movement but no dated sailing log or separate ministry scene in Neapolis.

events.title: Lydia and the prison episode
events.summary: Acts recounts Lydia, the enslaved girl, imprisonment and the jailer.

study.context: Philippi pairs Lydia's welcome and hospitality with later conflict, imprisonment and the jailer's household. These scenes trace the formation of relationships as well as the public consequences of the message.

events.title: Passing Amphipolis
events.summary: The city is named as a transit point.
events.qualification: No separate teaching episode is reported here.

study.context: Amphipolis is mentioned as a town passed through on the way to Thessalonica. Acts does not narrate a sermon or the formation of a church there, so the entry remains a travel stage.

events.title: Passing Apollonia
events.summary: The next transit point precedes Thessalonica.
events.qualification: No separate teaching episode is reported here.

study.context: Apollonia, like Amphipolis, is named on the passing itinerary rather than described as a separate preaching venue. The named settlement should not be taken as proof of an otherwise unmentioned church.

events.title: Scripture discussion and opposition
events.summary: Synagogue teaching is followed by unrest involving Jason.

study.context: At Thessalonica Paul reasons from Scripture about the Messiah's suffering and resurrection. Some respond while others oppose the new community, making this episode more than a geographic waypoint.

events.title: Examining the Scriptures
events.summary: The Berean response is followed by renewed opposition and Paul's departure.

study.context: At Berea people examine the Scriptures carefully and opposition follows from Thessalonica. Paul's departure is distinguished from Silas and Timothy remaining, so a single route line for the whole team would be misleading.

events.title: Speaking in Athens
events.summary: Paul teaches in public settings and addresses the Areopagus audience.
events.qualification: Acts 17:14-15 names Paul's arrival at Athens after leaving Berea but does not fix his precise transit path. Published GIS analysis compares plausible reconstructions rather than establishing one certain itinerary; companion movements and letter chronology require separate analysis.

study.context: In Athens Paul addresses an audience familiar with multiple philosophical traditions and speaks of the Creator, repentance and resurrection. Acts does not state his precise route from Berea or resolve the separate movements of his companions.

events.title: Work and teaching at Corinth
events.summary: Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla; Acts also narrates the Gallio hearing.

study.context: At Corinth Paul works alongside Aquila and Priscilla, teaches and encounters opposition. Acts mentions an eighteen-month period, but this does not establish every intermediate journey or an exact total regional itinerary.

events.title: Departure via Cenchreae
events.summary: The sailing departure includes a notice about a vow.

study.context: Cenchreae is part of the departure account that also mentions a vow. The passage's grammatical subject deserves care; the geographical stage is established more firmly than some readings of who made the vow.

events.title: A brief Ephesian visit
events.summary: Paul speaks in the synagogue and leaves, intending to return.

study.context: At Ephesus Paul reasons in the synagogue but does not extend this visit. His intention to return distinguishes this brief scene from the extended Ephesian ministry narrated later.

events.title: Landing at Caesarea
events.summary: The narrative names Caesarea before a church greeting.

study.context: The travellers land at Caesarea before Paul goes up to greet a church and then returns to Antioch. Caesarea is explicit, whereas the intermediate church's city is not named in Acts 18:22.

events.title: Greeting an unnamed church
events.summary: A church visit intervenes before the return to Antioch.
events.qualification: Acts 18:22 says Paul went up and greeted the church after landing at Caesarea, but does not name the church's city. Jerusalem is a common interpretation of 'went up', not an explicit place-name in this verse. This stage remains unpinned.

study.context: The unnamed church is frequently taken to be Jerusalem because Acts says Paul 'went up'. That is an inference, not the written place name, and no Jerusalem pin has been added for this stage.

events.title: Back at Antioch
events.summary: Acts records Paul's return to Antioch.

study.context: Paul returns to Antioch for an unspecified period before setting out again. This endpoint separates the second narrative journey unit from subsequent strengthening of disciples in Galatia and Phrygia.

events.title: Leaving Antioch again
events.summary: After a stay, Paul departs on another round of visits.

study.context: The new departure begins after Paul's return to Antioch. Acts 18:23 joins this visit to his continuing responsibility to strengthen disciples, rather than presenting a fresh commissioning ceremony with a fixed departure date.

events.title: Strengthening disciples inland
events.summary: The regional account names Galatia and Phrygia.

study.context: Galatia and Phrygia are regional terms in Acts 18:23. Their appearance underscores encouragement of existing communities, but the account neither lists each visited town nor settles the disputed geographical scope of Galatia.

events.title: The inland approach to Ephesus
events.summary: Paul passes through inland country before reaching Ephesus.

study.context: Paul reaches Ephesus after travelling through the inland country. Luke contrasts him with Apollos, who has appeared in the preceding narrative; the passage does not give named intermediate roads or stages.

events.title: The extended Ephesian ministry
events.summary: Acts narrates teaching, unusual events and the later disturbance connected with Artemis.
events.qualification: Apollos' travels in Acts 18:24-28 are not added as visits made by Paul.

study.context: At Ephesus, teaching moves from the synagogue to the hall of Tyrannus after opposition. Luke also records the encounter with the sons of Sceva, public renunciation of magic and the silversmiths' disturbance. These episodes concern discipleship and the city's economy as well as Paul's duration there.

events.title: Encouraging disciples in Macedonia
events.summary: Paul leaves after the disturbance and travels through Macedonia.

study.context: Paul encourages believers in Macedonia after the disturbance at Ephesus. Acts compresses several communities into a regional summary; recalling earlier Macedonian encounters helps readers follow the relationships without turning each possible city into a documented stop.

events.title: Three months in Greece
events.summary: A plot changes Paul's intended sailing departure.

study.context: Acts 20:2-3 describes a three-month stay in Greece and a plot that changes the planned departure. Although Corinth is often proposed as the main setting, it is not named in these verses, so the study remains geographically qualified.

events.title: Return through Macedonia
events.summary: Paul returns through Macedonia rather than taking the planned direct sailing.

study.context: A discovered plot prompts Paul to return through Macedonia instead of sailing as planned. Acts 20:4 names several companions, but the text should not be flattened into proof that every companion followed precisely the same route on every leg.

events.title: Departure after Unleavened Bread
events.summary: The sailing account resumes from Philippi.
events.qualification: Acts names Philippi; an otherwise unmentioned departure port is not substituted.

study.context: The narrative says the party sails from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and joins others at Troas. The festival supplies relative narrative timing, not an independently established year or a named departure quay.

events.title: A week at Troas
events.summary: The gathering includes the account of Eutychus.

study.context: During a gathering at Troas, Eutychus falls from an upper window and is taken up alive after Paul attends to him. The account emphasises the gathered community, the extended conversation and their consolation, not only an incident on a travel schedule.

events.title: Paul rejoins the ship
events.summary: Paul travels overland while his companions sail to Assos.
events.qualification: Acts 20:13 distinguishes Paul's journey by land to Assos from his companions' sailing there. The plotted sequence must not imply that Paul sailed the preceding leg.

study.context: Luke distinguishes the companions sailing to Assos from Paul, who intends to travel there by land before boarding with them. That textual distinction is essential: a continuous ship-track through this leg would misrepresent Paul's actual movement in the account.

events.title: Arrival at Mitylene
events.summary: After taking Paul aboard, the company reaches Mitylene.

study.context: After Paul rejoins the party at Assos, they proceed to Mitylene. This is an explicitly named stage in an otherwise compressed maritime itinerary, without an account of a sermon or independently located anchorage in the town.

events.title: Sailing opposite Chios
events.summary: The account describes passing the island, without reporting a landing.
events.qualification: Acts 20:15 says the ship sailed opposite Chios; it does not describe landing there. This stage remains offshore and unpinned.

study.context: Acts 20:15 says the party came opposite Chios, not that they landed on the island. An offshore passing reference should be read as a navigational description and kept distinct from the later arrival at Samos.

events.title: Arrival at Samos
events.summary: Samos is the next named stage of the voyage.
events.qualification: Acts 20:15 reports that the travellers touched at Samos. The map's marker locates only the island generally, not a particular ancient quay or a reconstructed sailing track.

study.context: The travellers reach Samos after passing opposite Chios. The island is named, but the canonical passage does not supply the quay, full approach route or exact arrival position represented by a modern island-scale marker.

events.title: Meeting the Ephesian elders
events.summary: Paul summons the elders to Miletus for his farewell address.
events.qualification: The elders come from Ephesus to Paul. Their travel is not plotted as a new Ephesian visit by Paul.

study.context: Paul summons Ephesian elders to Miletus instead of entering Ephesus again. His farewell looks back on service, warns of danger to the community and commends the elders to God; the travel decision and the pastoral charge are integral to the scene.

events.title: The next sailing stage: Cos
events.summary: The departure from Miletus leads to Cos.

study.context: Cos is named in a rapid itinerary after the farewell at Miletus. Acts gives the next sailing stage, not a distinct evangelistic episode or a specific island harbour; the departure's significance also lies in the emotional parting just narrated.

events.title: On to Rhodes
events.summary: The voyage continues to Rhodes.

study.context: The sea journey continues through Rhodes on the way to Patara. This is a sequential navigational notice rather than a record of missionary work at Rhodes or evidence for the precise path the vessel followed.

events.title: Changing ships at Patara
events.summary: The travellers find a ship bound for Phoenicia.

study.context: At Patara the party finds a ship crossing towards Phoenicia. Acts distinguishes this change of vessel from later sighting of Cyprus; the separate stages should not be collapsed into an imagined direct trip with known ports throughout.

events.title: Passing Cyprus offshore
events.summary: Cyprus is sighted as the ship continues towards Syria.

study.context: Cyprus appears to the travellers' left as they sail towards Syria. The island is a navigational sighting rather than a narrated landing, so a visible marker is deliberately withheld for this offshore stage.

events.title: Seven days with disciples at Tyre
events.summary: The ship unloads and the company meets local disciples.

study.context: At Tyre the ship unloads and believers host the travellers for seven days. Their warning concerning Jerusalem and their farewell with families praying on the beach turn a port stop into an account of solidarity and discernment.

events.title: A day at Ptolemais
events.summary: The travellers greet fellow believers and stay briefly.

study.context: Ptolemais is a brief visit in which the travellers greet fellow believers for one day. Luke's brevity is itself a limit: the text does not document an extended ministry or a detailed itinerary within the town.

events.title: Philip's household and Agabus
events.summary: The stay includes Agabus' warning before the ascent towards Jerusalem.

study.context: At Caesarea, Philip's household welcomes the company and Agabus acts out a warning about Paul's coming imprisonment. The different reactions to these warnings raise a question of discernment, not a directly mapped detour away from Jerusalem.

events.title: Arrival at Jerusalem
events.summary: The company travels inland and receives a welcome.
events.qualification: No precise road, lodging position or calendar date is supplied by this map.

study.context: Paul and his companions continue from Caesarea to Jerusalem and receive a welcome from believers. Luke describes companions and lodging arrangements in the surrounding verses, but not an exact road, address or date for the arrival.

events.title: Departure in custody
events.summary: Prisoners embark for Italy.
events.qualification: The port is inferred from the preceding Caesarea custody setting, not named in these embarkation verses.

study.context: The custody voyage follows Paul's extended imprisonment and appeal. Acts 27 introduces the centurion Julius and a ship from Adramyttium; Caesarea as the embarkation setting is inferred from the preceding custody narrative, not named in 27:1-2 itself.

events.title: Friends at Sidon
events.summary: Julius permits a visit with friends.

study.context: At Sidon, Julius allows Paul to visit friends and receive their care. The small episode gives a human dimension to a guarded prisoner voyage and must not be confused with Paul travelling free or making an independent missionary visit.

events.title: Sheltered passage by Cyprus
events.summary: Contrary winds affect the sailing.

study.context: Contrary winds lead the ship to sail under the lee of Cyprus. The passage indicates a weather-driven change in sailing conditions, not an island landing or a traced coastal route verified by modern navigational reconstruction.

events.title: Across the coastal sea
events.summary: The passage leads towards Lycia.

study.context: The account mentions sailing across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia before reaching Myra. These are coastal orientation terms; the text does not give named intermediate disembarkations, dates or coordinates along that waterway.

events.title: A change of ship
events.summary: The centurion finds an Alexandrian vessel bound for Italy.

study.context: At Myra, Julius transfers the prisoners to an Alexandrian ship bound for Italy. 'Alexandrian' identifies the vessel's association and direction, not proof that Paul travelled to Alexandria during this voyage.

events.title: Difficulty off Cnidus
events.summary: The wind prevents further progress on the intended course.

study.context: Slow sailing and contrary winds bring the ship off Cnidus, but the text does not say it landed there. The stage matters because the vessel redirects towards Crete after the failed progress on its intended course.

events.title: Shelter along Crete
events.summary: The ship sails in the lee of Crete.

study.context: The ship passes Salmone and works along Crete with difficulty. Luke depicts sailing under the island's shelter rather than a known overland visit; exact wind histories and modern plotted routes remain reconstructions.

events.title: A decision at Fair Havens
events.summary: Paul warns against continuing; the company seeks another winter harbour.
events.qualification: Acts 27:8 identifies Fair Havens as a reached anchorage. Phoenix appears in Acts 27:12 as an intended winter harbour, not a stop the narrative says the ship reached. The harbour decision is not a precise sailing route.

study.context: Fair Havens is reached, and Paul warns against further sailing after the dangerous season has begun. Most favour reaching Phoenix for winter, but Acts 27:12 names that harbour as a proposed destination, not a recorded arrival.

events.title: Securing the boat
events.summary: The storm drives the vessel past Cauda.
events.qualification: Acts 27:13-16 reports a favourable wind followed by a violent northeaster and passage in the lee of Cauda. The text does not provide a navigational track or an actual landing on Cauda; this is an offshore stage.

study.context: A brief favourable wind gives way to a violent northeaster that drives the vessel near Cauda, where the crew struggles to secure the boat. Cauda is a sheltered offshore passage, not evidence of landing on the island or fixing an exact track.

events.title: Drifting in the storm
events.summary: Cargo is discarded; Paul encourages the company.
events.qualification: Acts 27:17-26 reports the danger of the Syrtis, storm-driven movement, jettisoned cargo and Paul's assurance, but gives no coordinates or measured heading. The Syrtis was feared, not visited, and the drift is not pinned.

study.context: The storm forces protective measures, jettisoned cargo and prolonged uncertainty. Paul recounts an assurance that the passengers will survive while the ship is lost; the feared Syrtis is not a destination and the drift cannot be pinned from Acts alone.

events.title: Soundings and anchors
events.summary: The sailors suspect land is near and take soundings.
events.qualification: Acts 27:27-38 describes soundings and anchoring during the fourteenth night, without a named surveyed bay or precise offshore position. A traditional reconstruction is not a location verified by the text.

study.context: On the fourteenth night the sailors take soundings, drop anchors and attempt to manage the vessel while Paul urges everyone to eat. The measurements are part of the narrative but do not identify a verified modern offshore coordinate.

events.title: The ship is lost
events.summary: The company reaches shore from the breaking vessel.
events.qualification: Acts 27:39-44 describes an unidentified bay, beach, shoal and wreck. Acts identifies the island as Malta only after the survivors reach shore (28:1). The shipwreck is intentionally unpinned.

study.context: When daylight comes the sailors see an unfamiliar bay and try to beach the vessel, which breaks apart. The narrative separates the shipwreck scene in Acts 27 from the identification of the island as Malta in 28:1; no particular beach is proven.

events.title: Welcome on Malta
events.summary: The islanders offer shelter; Acts recounts the snake episode.
events.qualification: Acts 28:1 names Malta after the wreck. The island identification is explicit, but Acts 27:39-28:1 does not establish which modern bay or beach was the wreck location.

study.context: After reaching shore the survivors learn that the island is Malta. Luke relates local hospitality and the snake incident, but the named island does not establish which modern bay held the wreck, or where each event took place.

events.title: Hospitality and healing
events.summary: Publius receives the travellers; Acts recounts healings.

study.context: Publius welcomes the group, and Acts describes the healing of his father and others on Malta. These encounters are narrated after the wreck and are distinct from attempts to locate a specific shoreline or prove a later commemorative site.

events.title: Departure after winter
events.summary: After three months, the company boards another Alexandrian ship.

study.context: After three months on Malta, the company departs in another Alexandrian ship that had wintered there. The ship's figurehead and origin are vessel details; neither establishes Paul's visit to Alexandria or a precise winter calendar.

events.title: Three days at Syracuse
events.summary: The voyage resumes with a stay at Syracuse.

study.context: The travellers stop at Syracuse for three days. Luke provides the duration and place name, but does not narrate a sermon or identify a landing facility, so the visit should not acquire an invented ministry episode.

events.title: Arrival at Rhegium
events.summary: A changed wind precedes the next sailing.

study.context: At Rhegium the party pauses before a favourable south wind carries the vessel onward. The named harbour illustrates the continued importance of weather even after Malta, without proving every point of the crossing.

events.title: A week with believers
events.summary: The company stays with fellow believers.

study.context: At Puteoli, believers invite the travellers to stay a week. Hospitality reappears at the end of the maritime journey, showing social continuity between communities even while Paul remains bound for Rome.

events.title: Welcome on the approach to Rome
events.summary: Believers come out to meet Paul.
events.qualification: These meeting points follow the approach towards Rome; Acts does not supply a complete measured road itinerary.

study.context: Believers from Rome travel out as far as the Forum of Appius to meet Paul, who takes courage at their arrival. These are named meeting places in a road approach, not proof of the exact course or pace of every segment.

events.title: Another meeting on the approach
events.summary: The narrative also names Three Taverns.
events.qualification: These meeting points follow the approach towards Rome; Acts does not supply a complete measured road itinerary.

study.context: Three Taverns is also named among the places where believers came out to welcome Paul. The two meeting points describe a developing reception along the approach, not two unrelated arrivals in Rome.

events.title: Arrival under guard
events.summary: Paul is allowed separate lodging with a soldier.

study.context: On arrival in Rome, Paul is allowed lodging under a soldier's guard. The detail marks a change from dangerous transit to constrained residence; it does not indicate release or an independently known Roman street address.

events.title: Teaching in Rome
events.summary: Acts closes with discussions and an extended period of teaching.

study.context: Acts closes with Paul explaining the hope of Israel to Jewish leaders and welcoming listeners while under restriction. The final two-year notice describes continued proclamation, but the book does not narrate a subsequent release, execution or additional journey.

pleiades.title: Pleiades contributors, selected ancient place records
pleiades.scope: Ancient place identification and representative geography; not evidence of a visit by Paul.

natural-earth.title: Natural Earth, 1:110m land
natural-earth.scope: Modern low-resolution coastal orientation only. Small islands may be omitted; no historical borders.

issues.title: Journey groupings and dates
issues.description: First, second and third journey are conventional study labels. Acts supplies narrative sequences and some durations, not a complete modern calendar.

issues.title: Regional language and Galatia
issues.description: The regional phrases do not settle every town, road or the north/south Galatian reconstruction. Regional stages remain unpinned.

issues.title: The church in Acts 18:22
issues.description: Acts 18:22 does not name the city of the church Paul greets. Jerusalem is a common inference from the travel wording, not an explicit place-name here. No Jerusalem pin is added for this entry.

sourceLinks.title: Crossway ESV, Acts 18:18-22
sourceLinks.scope: The published verse names Caesarea and Antioch, but not the city of the intervening church; a Jerusalem destination remains interpretative.

issues.title: Greece is not a named third-journey Corinth stop
issues.description: Acts 20:2-3 names Greece. Corinth is commonly reconstructed as the main setting, but is not named in these verses and receives no third-journey pin on that basis.

issues.title: Island references and textual variants
issues.description: Opposite Chios and sighting Cyprus do not establish landings. Island markers elsewhere give only island-scale orientation. Trogyllium, included by some textual witnesses and translations of Acts 20:15, is not silently added to the common itinerary; manuscript comparison requires separate textual work.

sourceLinks.title: Acts 20:15, ESV publisher text and manuscript footnote
sourceLinks.scope: Documents the manuscript addition at Trogyllium; it does not establish a precise landing coordinate.

sourceLinks.title: Crossway ESV, Acts 20:13-38
sourceLinks.scope: Distinguishes Paul's land approach to Assos, passage opposite Chios, touching at Samos and the Miletus meeting. This is narrative, not a surveyed sea track.

issues.title: Derbe and Lystra location precision
issues.description: Pleiades representative points are provisional orientation. The Derbe candidate and separate undetermined Derbe record are kept distinct in the local source extract. A point cannot establish where a narrated event happened.

issues.title: Voyage, storm and wreck limitations
issues.description: This is not labelled a fourth missionary journey. The embarkation at Caesarea follows the preceding custody narrative; Acts 27:1-2 itself does not name the departure port. Phoenix is an intended winter harbour, not a reached stop. Adramyttium and Alexandria describe ships, not visits by Paul. The storm, soundings and wreck remain unpinned. Malta uses only an island-scale marker; no traditional wreck bay is asserted as certain.

sourceLinks.title: Crossway ESV, Acts 27
sourceLinks.scope: Names the reached Fair Havens, planned Phoenix, Cauda lee, offshore storm and unnamed wreck approach. Does not demonstrate a specific modern wreck bay.

sourceLinks.title: Crossway ESV, Acts 27-28:16
sourceLinks.scope: Acts identifies Malta after the wreck, not the exact geographical location of the wreck.

issues.title: Intended harbour, forced drift and island identification
issues.description: The narrative distinguishes Fair Havens, the proposed but unreached Phoenix winter harbour, the lee of Cauda, a storm-driven unlocated drift and an unnamed wreck bay. Malta is named as the island of arrival only after landfall. The route remains schematic and cannot be reverse-engineered into exact coordinates from Acts alone.

sourceLinks.title: Crossway ESV, Acts 27-28
sourceLinks.scope: Primary narrative comparison for reached, planned, offshore and unlocated settings; not an external maritime reconstruction.

issues.title: Berea to Athens: reconstructed route, not a recorded road
issues.description: Acts 17:14-15 narrates Paul's departure from Berea and arrival at Athens without fixing intervening roads or a definite sea crossing. A peer-reviewed GIS study analyses plausible alternatives and companion movements; one inferred route must not be treated as an explicit biblical statement or independently verified ancient track.

sourceLinks.title: Altena et al. (2021), GIS as a heuristic tool to interpret ancient historiography, Transactions in GIS
sourceLinks.scope: Peer-reviewed reconstruction study of Berea-to-Athens route uncertainty and companions; not proof of a unique historical route.

sourceLinks.title: Crossway ESV, Acts 17
sourceLinks.scope: Primary narrative for Berea, departure and Athens.

issues.title: Warnings on the journey to Jerusalem and Paul's decision
issues.description: Acts 20:22-24, 21:4 and 21:10-14 record Paul's compulsion to continue and the responses of disciples and Agabus who anticipate his suffering. Readers differ over how to reconcile the Spirit's warnings and the companions' appeals not to go. The site records both textual contexts without claiming an uncontroversial harmonisation.

sourceLinks.title: Alan J. Thompson, Acts commentary, The Gospel Coalition
sourceLinks.scope: Published commentary on Acts 21:1-14, including divergent understandings of warnings and the decision to continue; interpretive resource, not independent historical evidence.

issues.title: The voyage's literary meaning is not a surveyed sailing route
issues.description: Acts 27-28 contains storm, prisoner, maritime and providential themes alongside geographical names. Literary interpretation and historical maritime reconstruction address different questions. The published article abstract considers an imperial reading of the nautical narrative, without certifying an exact ancient route or wreck location.

sourceLinks.title: Warren Carter, Aquatic Display: Navigating the Roman Imperial World in Acts 27, New Testament Studies 62 (2016), 79-96
sourceLinks.scope: Peer-reviewed academic literary interpretation of Acts 27-28.10; abstract consulted, not the full text. This is not a geographic survey or proof of a wreck site.

studyCoverage.scope: All 83 of 83 Pauline stages, covering the first, second and third conventional missionary journeys and the separate prisoner voyage to Rome, have original Scripture-based study contexts and related canonical reading passages.
studyCoverage.method: AI-assisted original Scripture-first editorial reading and cross-passage comparison. Geographical limitations, groupings, text variants and other research cautions remain visible; not a certification of exact sailing paths, city visits, textual chronology or archaeological site matches.
studyCoverage.limit: Scripture reading aids are not independent specialist historical reviews; published academic interpretation of the Acts voyage is not an independently surveyed route. The wider flagship historical audit and specialist consultation remain open.
